title: Four Ways to Know
concept: After this one you can make a call about a voice from what you see and hear, and then check it three more ways.
bookIdea: Berne listed four ways of recognising an ego state: behavioural (what you see and hear), social (how others respond), historical (how the person was as a child) and phenomenological (living the old moment again). Behavioural comes first and matters most, and the other three act as checks.
bookSource: TA Today, ch. 5; Transactional Analysis in Psychotherapy, ch. 7

opener.setting: Thursday, 13:00, Halden canteen. You have just sat down at the long table with your tray.

lines.text: “Right, lunch is lunch. Nobody talks shop until the hatch is clear.”
lines.cue: stirring his tea, not looking up

opener.ask: When a line sounds like a rule or a fear dressed as a fact, what do you check first, and what can back up your call?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: How this one works: there are four ways to check a voice. What the person does, how the room answers, where it came from in their past, and whether they can live it again. Read each clue and say which kind it is.

items.text: Daniel folds his arms and taps the table twice before he speaks.
items.cue: a posture you can see from across the table
items.why: This is what you can see and hear right now. Folded arms and a tap on the table are how a Boss looks from outside, so it is evidence about what he is doing. It is the first clue to read, and the main one.

traps.1: How people answer would be the room's reply, such as Clara going quiet. Here the clue is his own posture, before anyone has replied.
traps.2: Where it came from would be a story about the past, such as his father at the dinner table. Folded arms and a tap happen now, in this room.
traps.3: Reliving it would mean Daniel going back into an old scene and feeling all of it again. A posture you can see across the table is something he is doing now.

items.example:
A train platform, a guard before the doors close: he folds his arms and taps his whistle twice. “Nobody stands by the yellow line.”
The posture is the clue. The rule is about who is in charge.

items.text: Clara looks down at her plate, and the table goes quiet for five seconds after he finishes.
items.cue: a silence that the whole table joins
items.why: This is the room's reply. People tend to answer from the voice that pairs with the one they were spoken to in, and a Boss often gets a quiet Kid back. The silence is a check on the call, since it shows what the speech did to the room.

traps.0: What it does would be Daniel's own posture. Here the clue is what Clara did after he spoke, so it is how people answer.
traps.2: Where it came from needs a past. Nothing in a silent plate tells us about anyone's history.
traps.3: Reliving it would mean Clara going back into an old scene and feeling it all over again. A look at her plate is something she is doing now.

items.example:
A family WhatsApp group, a long message about the holiday plan: four people read it, and nobody types for ten minutes. Then a cousin posts a sticker.
The silence is the reply, and the sticker is a way of changing the subject.

items.text: Daniel says his father used the same words, in the same tone, at the dinner table when Daniel was small.
items.cue: a story about his childhood, told as if it explains everything
items.why: This is history: how the person was as a child and who raised him. If he can name whose words he is copying, that backs up the call. It is a check, and it does not replace watching what he does now.

traps.0: What it does would be what he is doing at the table now. This clue is a story about his childhood, rather than a move he is making.
traps.1: How people answer would be the room's reply. Here the clue is an old memory that nobody at the table has answered yet.
traps.3: Reliving it would mean Daniel back inside that dinner, feeling it as it was. Reporting what his father used to say is history, and he is telling it from the outside.

items.example:
A grandfather at a family dinner: “In my time, nobody left the table until the elders had finished.” He heard it from his own grandfather, and he says it every holiday weekend.
The line is older than the dinner. That is what history looks like.

items.text: Daniel stops mid-sentence. “Funny. When I say it like that I can see the kitchen again. Dad at the head of the table, me at eight, holding my fork very still. My stomach has gone tight, right now.”
items.cue: he looks at nothing, and his voice has gone younger
items.why: He is back in the scene and feeling it at full strength, as if it were happening. The books use this check in a special sense, and it is the deepest of the four. It usually comes up in therapy, and it only happens when the person is ready.

traps.0: What it does would be a posture or a tone you could watch from across the table. What Daniel describes is what he is going through inside.
traps.1: How people answer would be the room's reply. Nobody has said anything yet, so there is nothing to read there.
traps.2: Where it came from would be Daniel telling the story from outside, such as “My father used to say that.” He is not reporting the kitchen, he is in it.

items.example:
A woman in a quiet corner of a family wedding, talking about her old school.
She stops, goes still and says, “I can smell the corridor. My hands are cold, and I'm waiting to be called on.”
She is no longer remembering the day. She is living it again.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: One main clue, one check. Read what the person does first, then the check in the cue. Pick the voice they point to.

items.text: “Junior devs today just don't have the discipline we had.”
items.cue: What it does: folded arms and a flat voice. How people answer: nobody at the table argues.
items.why: The behaviour comes first: the body lays down a rule. The room's reply backs it up, because the table goes quiet rather than checking the claim. This line has no numbers in it, so it is a Boss's rule wearing the clothes of a fact.

traps.1: The Pilot would bring numbers: “Here are the hire dates and the review scores.” This line brings none, and nobody at the table checked it.
traps.2: The Kid would sound scared and small: “Maybe I'm the one who's rubbish at this.” Daniel is blaming the juniors, not doubting himself.

items.example:
A cricket club dinner, the chairman after a loss: “Youngsters today can't handle pressure.” He folds his arms, and the players look at their boots.
Two clues point the same way: the posture and the silence. Neither one is a score.

items.text: “We tried caching it in 2023, and it broke the invoices.”
items.cue: What it does: calm and specific, pointing at no one. How people answer: Clara asks which invoices, and Daniel asks for the ticket number.
items.why: The behaviour comes first: calm, specific and aimed at no one. The room's reply backs it up, because people ask for details they can use. The date and the result also mean the claim can be checked, which is what a Pilot invites.

traps.0: The Boss would make it a rule: “We tried it, so we never try it again.” The fact stays the same, but the verdict has become a rule, and the room would go quiet instead of asking questions.
traps.2: The Kid would hear “it can't be done” and go small: “I don't think we should try, sorry.” Omar's line has no fear in it, and the room is asking questions rather than soothing him.

items.example:
A college project group, a student: “We tried a shared spreadsheet in March, and the marks went missing.” She shows the date in the email thread.
Even when it sounds like a no, a dated memory is a fact.

items.text: “Everyone here is cleverer than me. There's no point me suggesting anything.”
items.cue: What it does: a small voice, eyes on her plate, shoulders in. Where it came from: she says her older brother used to finish her sentences and call her “the slow one”.
items.why: The behaviour comes first: a small voice, eyes down, shoulders in. Her history backs it up, because the “slow one” label is an old family one she still replays. The line sounds like a plain fact, but nothing in it can be checked, so it is an old fear speaking.

traps.0: The Boss would aim a verdict at someone else: “Nobody here bothers to think.” Clara's line lowers herself, and her voice is small, not hard.
traps.1: The Pilot would say what she knows and what she doesn't: “I have two ideas and I haven't tested either.” Her line can't be checked, and her posture says the same thing as her words: small.

items.example:
A student after a maths test: “Everyone's cleverer than me, there's no point asking.”
She is looking at the floor. At primary school a teacher once called her “hopeless at numbers”, and she has never put the label down.

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Daniel's line, four ways. Each bin is one voice. Put each clue in the bin it points to, then read the why.

items.prompt: Put each clue into the voice it points to.

items.text: What it does: arms folded, a flat voice and a tap on the table.
items.why: What he does points to the Boss: a rule laid down in a fixed tone, the posture of someone who expects agreement. This is the main clue.

items.text: How people answer: the table goes quiet, and nobody checks the claim.
items.why: The silence is the room answering a Boss with a Kid. When people go quiet instead of checking, the voice that spoke was usually the Boss.

items.text: Where it came from: his father said the same thing, in the same tone, at the dinner table.
items.why: History shows the line was learned from someone else. It is a recording, and it says nothing about whether the juniors are any good.

items.text: Reliving it: when he repeats the line slowly, he hears his father's voice coming out of his own mouth and sees the table where it was first said.
items.why: He is living the moment he took the voice on. It is the deepest check, and it points to the Boss: he is copying his father.

items.text: What he says about himself: “I'm just being rational, that's all.”
items.why: His own account points to the Pilot, because he says he is being reasonable. A person's description of himself is not one of the four ways, and it can differ from what he is doing, so it cannot outrank the clues above.

items.text: What it does, a second later: he laughs at his own line and glances round the table to see who will join in.
items.why: A laugh at his own line, with a look round for company, is the Kid wanting the room to like it. Voices can shift within a minute, so the call has to be made line by line.

items.text: Daniel insists he is “just being rational”. You saw his folded arms and flat voice, and the table went quiet. Which should count most?
options: His own account, because nobody knows his mind better
What he does first, with the room's reply and his history as checks
His history alone, because the past decides the voice
items.why: Start with what you can see and hear. It is the main clue, though no single clue settles a call. How people answer and where the voice came from are checks on it, and reliving it is the deepest check. The more of them that line up, the surer the call.

traps.0: His account is a claim, and a person can feel sure he is being reasonable while his body says otherwise. It can sit beside the other clues, but it does not outrank what you can see and hear.
traps.2: History is a useful check, but it only tells you where a voice could have come from. It cannot tell you which voice is talking right now.

items.example:
A teacher sees a pupil slumped at the back, speaking in a very quiet voice. She doesn't decide yet.
She notices how the other pupils treat him, and later asks his mum what he was like at six.
The slump started the call, and the rest checked it.

debrief.nadia: There are four ways to check a voice: what the person does, how the room answers, where it came from, and whether they can live it again. Start with what you can see and hear, because that is the main clue. The other three are checks, and the more of them that line up, the surer you can be. A person's own account of himself is not one of the four.
debrief.bookNote: The books call these the behavioural, social, historical and phenomenological diagnoses. Berne says behavioural comes first and matters most, and the other three act as checks. He uses phenomenological in a special sense: living the old moment again at full strength.

reflection.prompt: Think of a line someone said to you this week that you took as a fact. What did you see and hear when they said it, and what could you check afterwards?
